MetricsGovernance  
People killed in armed conflicts in each country, by year.
This counts the people killed in armed conflicts in a country in a year: soldiers and civilians, in wars between states, civil wars, fighting between armed groups and one-sided violence against civilians. Deaths are assigned to the country where they happened. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) records every event from news reports, NGO and UN sources and other documents, and gives its best estimate; Our World in Data republishes it. The current year is left out until it is complete.

Title: Life expectancy has continued to rise in the longest-lived countries
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Data Insights
Life expectancy has continued to rise in the longest-lived countries
January 08, 2025
Record national life expectancies have been climbing for over a century.
In 1840, Swedish women had a life expectancy of 46 years —the highest of any country recorded that year. By 1921, Australia held the record at 63 years.
For most of the 20th century, Iceland, Norway, Australia, and Sweden competed for the top position before being overtaken by Japan in 1984. Hong Kong and Japan have held the records since then.
These countries didn’t merely catch up; they’ve continued to push the limits higher.
Japan added six more years to female life expectancy between 1984 and 2010, rising from 80 to 86 years.
This remarkable rise has resulted from many advances in medicine, public health, and living standards —breaking many predictions of the “limits” of life expectancy.
Read more in our article about the rise of maximum life expectancy →

## Our latest Data Insights
See all Data Insights
*    Yesterday ### Population aging is pushing up Chile’s crude cancer death rate, even as age-adjusted rates are falling Esteban Ortiz-Ospina In Chile, the annual number of cancer deaths as a share of the total population has been rising for decades. From this, it would be easy to assume that cancer is getting worse. But the chances of dying from cancer at most ages are lower than they used to be. The missing piece is that the country’s population is changing quickly, and older people now make up a much larger share. That’s what the chart shows. The _crude_ cancer death rate, in red, counts registered cancer deaths per 100,000 people of all ages. This metric has been going up, reflecting the fact that cancer risks increase steeply with age, and the population has grown much older. The blue line, by contrast, shows the _age-adjusted_ rate. This metric removes the effect of aging by holding the age structure constant. This line has been falling for decades, which means that Chileans at almost every age are now less likely to die from cancer than people of the same age were in the past. The pattern we see in Chile is happening in many other countries, too, and is visible in the global estimates. Explore this same comparison country by country in our interactive chart  
*    November 3 ### Solar and wind power have grown quickly in Poland, but coal still dominates Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada The share of electricity produced by solar and wind in Poland more than doubled in just four years. In 2021, these renewable sources produced just 11% of its power; by 2025, this had risen to 25%. You can see this growth in the chart, based on electricity data from Ember. Solar and wind output, combined, grew very little in 2025, due to weak wind conditions. Solar output continued to grow, but it was barely enough to offset the decline in wind power. Poland still has one of the most coal-intensive electricity mixes in Europe, with coal producing 50% of its power. The country has committed to moving away from it in the next few decades; growth in solar and wind generation will play a key role in this. Explore energy sources across the world in our charts  

## Our latest Data Insights
*    October 31 ### One in ten people in the world is over 65 — how does this compare in the youngest and oldest countries? Hannah Ritchie One in four people in the world is younger than 15. Just one in ten is 65 or older. But there are huge differences in this distribution across countries. In the chart, I’ve shown these global figures alongside the country with the largest share of children, the Central African Republic, and the one with the largest share of older people, Japan. In the Central African Republic, half of the population is under 15. Being over 65 is pretty rare: just 2% of the population. Japan is the opposite. Being a child or adolescent puts you in the minority. Almost one-third of the population is 65 and older, and that share is growing quickly. These differences in age distribution matter a lot for a country’s infrastructure, socioeconomic conditions, and public spending — from pensions and healthcare to childcare and education. See how the age distribution of your own country compares to others across the world  
*    October 29 ### How is life at different levels of GDP per capita? Max Roser The chart shows the relationship between GDP (gross domestic product) per capita — a measure of average incomes in a country — and people’s living conditions. Where GDP per capita is higher, living conditions are far better in many ways. Where average incomes are higher, children die less often, fewer of them are born dead, mothers die less often, fewer children suffer from hunger, doctors can focus on fewer patients, people live longer, more people can read, children have better access to education and better learning outcomes, more people have access to electricity and clean drinking water, and people are happier with their lives. The disparity between countries with a low and a high GDP per capita is enormous. Looking at the first panel, for example, you can see that a child born in one of the poorest countries is more than 20 times as likely to die as a child born in one of the richest. In my article “What is growth?”, I have written about why a high GDP per capita is so important for our living standards and how economic growth is possible  

## Our latest Data Insights
*    October 27 ### In China, more than one in five workers is still employed in agriculture Esteban Ortiz-Ospina China makes and exports more goods than any other country. So, perhaps unsurprisingly, when I think about China’s economy, the first thing that comes to mind is manufacturing — increasingly at the technological frontier in electric vehicles, batteries, and solar panels. China’s position in manufacturing follows decades of economic transformation. The chart shows one aspect of this: the decline in agricultural employment. At the turn of the 21st century, around half of all Chinese workers were employed in agriculture. One generation later, that share had more than halved, reaching 22% in 2025. I find it striking how far the share of workers in agriculture has fallen, and just as striking how high it remains. Agriculture employs more than a fifth of China’s workers, while accounting for less than 7% of its GDP. Explore agricultural employment trends for all countries in our interactive chart  
*    October 24 ### The world is getting more of its electricity from renewables but less from nuclear power Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada If the world is to reduce its carbon emissions and tackle climate change, it needs to move away from fossil fuels to low-carbon power. Data Insights
Life expectancy has continued to rise in the longest-lived countries
January 08, 2025
Record national life expectancies have been climbing for over a century.
In 1840, Swedish women had a life expectancy of 46 years —the highest of any country recorded that year. By 1921, Australia held the record at 63 years.
For most of the 20th century, Iceland, Norway, Australia, and Sweden competed for the top position before being overtaken by Japan in 1984. Hong Kong and Japan have held the records since then.
These countries didn’t merely catch up; they’ve continued to push the limits higher.
Japan added six more years to female life expectancy between 1984 and 2010, rising from 80 to 86 years.
This remarkable rise has resulted from many advances in medicine, public health, and living standards —breaking many predictions of the “limits” of life expectancy.
Read more in our article about the rise of maximum life expectancy →

*    Yesterday ### Population aging is pushing up Chile’s crude cancer death rate, even as age-adjusted rates are falling Esteban Ortiz-Ospina In Chile, the annual number of cancer deaths as a share of the total population has been rising for decades. From this, it would be easy to assume that cancer is getting worse. But the chances of dying from cancer at most ages are lower than they used to be. The missing piece is that the country’s population is changing quickly, and older people now make up a much larger share. That’s what the chart shows. The _crude_ cancer death rate, in red, counts registered cancer deaths per 100,000 people of all ages. This metric has been going up, reflecting the fact that cancer risks increase steeply with age, and the population has grown much older. The blue line, by contrast, shows the _age-adjusted_ rate. This metric removes the effect of aging by holding the age structure constant. This line has been falling for decades, which means that Chileans at almost every age are now less likely to die from cancer than people of the same age were in the past. The pattern we see in Chile is happening in many other countries, too, and is visible in the global estimates. Explore this same comparison country by country in our interactive chart  
*    November 3 ### Solar and wind power have grown quickly in Poland, but coal still dominates Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada The share of electricity produced by solar and wind in Poland more than doubled in just four years. In 2021, these renewable sources produced just 11% of its power; by 2025, this had risen to 25%. You can see this growth in the chart, based on electricity data from Ember. Solar and wind output, combined, grew very little in 2025, due to weak wind conditions. Solar output continued to grow, but it was barely enough to offset the decline in wind power. Poland still has one of the most coal-intensive electricity mixes in Europe, with coal producing 50% of its power. The country has committed to moving away from it in the next few decades; growth in solar and wind generation will play a key role in this. Explore energy sources across the world in our charts

*    October 31 ### One in ten people in the world is over 65 — how does this compare in the youngest and oldest countries? Hannah Ritchie One in four people in the world is younger than 15. Just one in ten is 65 or older. But there are huge differences in this distribution across countries. Being a child or adolescent puts you in the minority. Almost one-third of the population is 65 and older, and that share is growing quickly. *    October 29 ### How is life at different levels of GDP per capita? Max Roser The chart shows the relationship between GDP (gross domestic product) per capita — a measure of average incomes in a country — and people’s living conditions. Where GDP per capita is higher, living conditions are far better in many ways. Where average incomes are higher, children die less often, fewer of them are born dead, mothers die less often, fewer children suffer from hunger, doctors can focus on fewer patients, people live longer, more people can read, children have better access to education and better learning outcomes, more people have access to electricity and clean drinking water, and people are happier with their lives. The disparity between countries with a low and a high GDP per capita is enormous. Looking at the first panel, for example, you can see that a child born in one of the poorest countries is more than 20 times as likely to die as a child born in one of the richest. In my article “What is growth?”, I have written about why a high GDP per capita is so important for our living standards and how economic growth is possible

## Data sources
#### James C. Riley – Estimates of Regional and Global Life Expectancy, 1800–2001
Historians and demographers have gone through considerable trouble to reconstruct life expectancy in the past in individual countries.
This overview collects information from a large body of that work and links estimates for historical populations to those provided by the United Nations, the World Bank, and other sources for 1950–2001. The result shows regional and global life expectancy at birth for selected years from 1800 to 2001. The bibliography of more than 700 sources is published separately on the web.
